channel.title: Manhattan on Gourmand Syndrome
channel.description: Recent content in Manhattan on Gourmand Syndrome

item.title: Soba Ulala
item.description: Soba Ulala is a new concept from the Hirohisa team, where it’s centered around house-made soba and how they carry forward their familiar restaurant flavors in a more relaxed a’la carte style. The former Michelin star restaurant will be moving to a new location, and this Thompson Street location converted to this concept. We were in in the Soho area, and I abruptly made the reservation for 5:30 PM for 2 on a Thursday evening at 5:15 PM. Reservations seem fairly easy to get, so thankfully it wasn’t too stressful.

item.title: Grandma's Home
item.description: The first Grandma’s Home opened in Hangzhou, which is the capital of China’s Zhejiang province. This location is the first American outpost of this popular Chinese chain. Zhejiang flavors tend to focus on seafood and local produce with a delicate, mellow sweetness with light soy sauce, Shaoxing wine, or local vinegars. It’s also different because it’s not as greasy as other Chinese regional foods. I made a reservation for this the day before, and it was very available. When we walked in around 5:30 PM, the restaurant was pretty empty, so perhaps reservations are unneeded.

item.title: Saverne
item.description: Saverne is Gabriel Kreuther’s modern wood-fired French brasserie using traditional techniques of letting wood flames add layers of smokiness to seasonal ingredients. Saverne actually opened a while ago around March 2026, but it closed just after 8 days due to mechanical issue. It just reopened in July 2026. Having been to Gabriel Kreuther, the chef’s Michelin 2-star restaurant, we were quite excited to see what he had in mind for a more casual outing. One of the main allures of the restaurant was that it has a wood-fire oven and grill where they cook your meats and then prepare your food. We made a reservation for 2 easily for 6 PM on a Friday evening.

item.title: Salswee
item.description: Shortly after Tenjou, we decided to look for desserts around the area. I stumbled onto this restaurant, and it reminded me a bit of [Lysee]({< relref “lysee” >}), where the desserts seem very interesting to look at. The restaurant is similar to many of the newer dessert places around the city, where you can look into the counter and pick the items that you want. From their website, they aim to make hyper-realistic fruit desserts with artisanal quality and unique flavor combinations.

item.title: Tenjou
item.description: Tenjou was on my list for a while. The menu looked pretty decent, and the prices weren’t ridiculous. One of the pictures showed the egg rice (omurice), which looked pretty good. As a general Japanese restaurant, it seemed to have plenty to offer in the Flatiron area, especially something for everyone. We stopped by while in the area without reservations, and it was very easy to walk in for 2 people.

item.title: L'abeille à Côté
item.description: L’abeille à Côte sits between 2 of its sibling restaurants, the Michelin-starred L’abeille and Muku. The host described to me that this particular restaurant was a French Japanese restaurant leaning more towards the Japanese side. Muku was a pure Japanese kaiseki, and L’abeille was a French Japanese leaning more towards French. The cuisine here is described with offering a playful interpretation of the refined. When I took a look at the menu, it was intriguing to see some of the dishes. I made a reservations a few days prior for 6 PM on a Friday evening for 2 people very easily.

item.title: S&P Lunch
item.description: S&P Lunch is located near Madison Park, which is where the original Shake Shack is located. They are known for its classic Jewish deli fare with a 1920s luncheonette vibe. This used to be “Eisenberg’s Sandwich Shop”, but that closed just right before the pandemic. In place, Eric Finkelstein and Matt Ross took over this space and decided to honor the original S&P Sandwich Shop that opened in this spot in 1928. We walked in on a late Saturday afternoon around 4:00 PM without needing to wait.

item.title: 5ive Spice
item.description: We were in the Nolita area doing some errands, and we ventured to this street looking for some food. There are many restaurants to pick from, but my partner did not want anything spicy or filling. From where we stood, I looked across the street, and I saw this pho place. We were also decently near the Lower East Side, but it started to rain and steered us towards eating at this restaurant. We walked in for 2 around 4:30 PM on a Saturday afternoon without reservations easily. As of this writing in addition to the Nolita location, they also have it in Gramercy and Park Slope.

item.title: Howoo
item.description: Howoo was on my list for some time, and my goodness my partner finally felt like eating Korean BBQ again. Normally, they are open to this, but they have not picked this cuisine for quite some time. I don’t remember why exactly I had Howoo on my list, but when it first opened, the pictures made it seem like it had good meats. One of our favorites, Yoon Haeundae Galbi, had excellent meat quality, and it was well worth the premium prices for good quality cuts. This one with their “set” menus appeared attractive in their own regard. We walked in for 2 at around 4:30 PM right before the swarm of people arrived.

item.title: Dean's
item.description: Dean’s comes from chef-owner Jess Shadbolt and co-owner/beverage director Annie Shi. The two were behind a restaurant called “King” in SoHo, and they pay homage to coastal heritage cooking with the name being an inspiration from “Dean Fryer”, who is a childhood fisherman from the chef’s hometown in Suffolk, England. This restaurant has been garnering some trends for a while because it is an ode to the British pub, and I had the opportunity to try this out. I walked in around 7:30 PM on a weekday evening and sat solo at the bar.

item.title: Torrisi
item.description: Torrisi is housed within the iconic Puck Building on Mulberry Street, right in the heart of Nolita. The restaurant comes from the Major Food Group, most well known for Carbone and The Grill. The one annoying part about this restaurant is how difficult it is to get a reservation. They seem to only release specific timeslots late in the evening (like after 10 PM), and none around the 5-6 PM. I was scouting for a few days, and so I opted for the lunch times on the weekend instead of trying for dinner on a weekday or weekend. After 3-4 tries, I was able to manually snipe a reservation for 12:00 PM on a Saturday. I took a look at the menu, and I noticed it was not too drastically different than dinner.

item.title: Park Ave Kitchen by David Burke
item.description: We were near Grand Central Terminal, and I had to make an improvised attempt to look for a restaurant nearby. For a Saturday evening, it was going to be difficult to look for something worthwhile and not too expensive. I ended up finding this restaurant just a few streets north of Grand Central. We walked in for 2 at around 6:30 PM, and the restaurant had nearly no patrons in there. We were told that the restaurant is more popular for breakfast and lunch than dinner. The restaurant opened in December 2023 and occupies a 8,700-square foot space that has an upscale sit-down dining and a fast casual cafe.

item.title: Luthun
item.description: Luthun is a restaurant that draws upon Chef Nahid Ahmed’s inspirations from traveling around the world and embracing his Indian Bengali heritage. He has spent time working in many kitchens around the world, and this is his restaurant. The reason I picked this restaurant was due to many reviewers saying the food is very good, arguably much better than some Michelin starred restaurants in the city. Also, making reservations was quite easy and not pretentiously bothersome. We made a reservation for 6:30 PM on a Friday night, and the meal lasted roughly 2.5 hours.

item.title: Opto
item.description: Opto has been on my list for quite a bit, and we just never really had an opportunity to try it out until now. The Flatiron area continues to experience turnover and restaurant transitions, and this Mediterranean place was the latest. When it first opened, reservations were definitely needed, but over time, it seemed the need thinned out. We were able to walk in for 2 at around 6:00 PM on a Sunday evening.

item.title: Via Quadronno
item.description: We were walking around in the upper east side along Madison Ave, where there are higher end shops. It has a slight Beverly Hills vibe, but my partner wanted to see something at the Ralph Lauren store. After, we desired for an early dinner, so I ended up finding this place because it had lasagna. Without any vetting, we walked in for 2 around 4:30 PM on a Saturday late afternoon.

item.title: Le Coucou
item.description: I actually went to Le Coucou many years ago, around 2017. In my previous notes, I said, “Amazing place. The baked alaska and veal tongue were really good. It’s also not too expensive.” and nothing more. Now many years later, I went here again with my partner to properly celebrate. Coincidentally the day we ate here is nearly their 10-year anniversary. Because reservations for 2 at 6:00 PM were easily obtained the same day, it was very hassle free and no pressure.

item.title: Bourbon and Branch
item.description: We were meeting a friend in town, so we frantically looked for a restaurant near their hotel. We stumbled onto this randomly because it offered burgers, which seemed like an easy success. Our friend previously lived in NYC, but they were under a budget. I was able to make a same day reservation for three people at 6 PM on a Sunday evening without any issues. The restaurant is located right across the street from Madison Square Garden.

item.title: Jean-Georges
item.description: Jean-Georges is a highly rated French-ish restaurant owned by Jean-Georges Vongerichten. It has garnered two Michelin Stars, and in his empire, this is his flagship restaurant. We’ve already been to several, including Jojo, Four Twenty Five, and The Fulton. This restaurant is also very easy to get a reservation a few days in advance, so you don’t really need to snipe unless you want a very popular time. Just a note that this is located across the street from Columbus Circle.

item.title: Iron Bar
item.description: The Iron Bar and Lounge is located in the middle of the Theater District along 8th Avenue and 45th Street. We walked into this restaurant because my partner was craving for a burger, and it was between this and Junior’s. Because the World Cup festivities have just begun, there were a lot of people inside just coming early to watch sports on TVs. We were able to walk with 2 people around 4:30 PM without any reservations.

item.title: The Independent
item.description: The Independent is a New American joint that is close to the Theater District. Because we had a show to catch and running out of options, we walked into this restaurant on a late Saturday afternoon without reservations. The restaurant has a pretty small menu, and it’s slightly different than your pub style food. For the price, we thought this could be a quick and good way to try this out.

item.title: Bartolo
item.description: Bartolo is a Madrid-style taverna in the West Village area, and it is a nod to chef/owner Ryan Bartlow’s nickname when he was working at Michelin-starred Akelarre in Spain. The restaurant when it opened was wide open for availability, but quickly became impossible without planning to get a reservation. Coincidentally the week prior, I was randomly trying to find a place to try, and I was able to book a reservation for 2 for 5:00 PM on a Friday evening. I was curious to see what this one had to offer considering we’ve been to several Spanish restaurants in the city already.

item.title: Cuerno
item.description: Cuerno has been on our list for quite a while. We ended up seeing an early afternoon show, so I was able to book this restaurant for 5 PM for 2 the day of. Cuerno is an authentic Mexican steakhouse known for fire-grilled prime steaks, bold Northern Mexican flavors, and refined dining. Outside of the restaurant, the whole area smells like grill and charcoal. When we entered, we checked in, but we had to stand around for a few minutes.

item.title: Shmone
item.description: Shmone is a Michelin-starred Greenwich Village restaurant, known for Chef Eyal Shani’s neo-Levantine cuisine. Although this is Mediterranean, I wanted to see how it represents Israeli and Middle Eastern. Keep in mind that Michelin Stars are awarded for the food alone. We were able to make a reservation a few weeks in advance without any issue. Do note that this is adjacent to their wine bar which is not their restaurant.

item.title: Grand Brasserie
item.description: Grand Brasserie is a large French restaurant located in the Grand Central Terminal. It’s situated in the historic Vanderbilt Hall. The main parts of the restaurant have an open area view to the Grand Central hall, so you can see the chandeliers and some of the nice subtleties of the terminal. The main interesting aspect of this restaurant is they have a “green room” which used to be the former Michelin Star restaurant “Agern” before it closed during the pandemic. I was easily able to make a reservation for 2 for 5:30 PM.

item.title: Txula Steak
item.description: Located at Mercado Little Spain, Txula Steak is chef Jose Andres love letter to Spain. He’s one of the chefs that has opened a bunch of restaurants, including Nubeluz, Zaytinya, and Oyamel to name a few. The Mercado Little Spain sits at ground level of mall next to the Vessel. You can enter thru the mall via Little Spain to get here, or enter at ground level off 30th St outside. We easily made reservations for 5:30 PM same day on Friday.
